sources.citation: Hey, Nicholas. 1903. An elementary grammar of the Nggerikudi language (North Queensland Ethnography Bulletin No. 6, rev. and ed. W. E. Roth). Brisbane: Government Printer. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement of word stress or accent anywhere in the grammar (whole text searched for accent/stress/emphasis/syllable/pronunciation/intonation; the preface only says the spelling follows the RGS 'Orthography of Geographical Names'). The single prosodic remark is expressive and sentence-level, at the end of section 31 'Exclamations' (p. 23): 'Note: Anger and intensity are expressed by prolonging the last syllable in the sentence.'

sources.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1981. The Mpakwithi dialect of Anguthimri. In R. M. W. Dixon & B. J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 2, 146-194. Canberra: ANU Press. (pp. 147-156 read)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Yangathimri stress. p. 149: Yangathimri 'closely related to Anguthimri, though still a distinct language', c. 100 lexical items remembered by the Mpakwithi consultant, 67.5% shared vocabulary; p. 153: palatal stop appears to be a genuine phoneme in Yangathimri. Anguthimri (not Yangathimri) stress, 2.3 pp. 155-156: first syllable and every alternate syllable stressed, final syllable never stressed; long vowels only in stressable syllables.

sources.citation: Hale, Kenneth L. 1966. [Northern Paman section] in O'Grady, Voegelin & Voegelin, Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Six. Anthropological Linguistics 8(2): 162-197.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Group-level Northern Paman stress shift to the second syllable (pp. 167-168) and Linngithigh rule (p. 179), but Yangathimri/Tjungundji is not among the 13 sampled varieties (p. 163) and is not mentioned; p. 165 notes Hey 1903 treated all coastal dialects 'from Cullen Pt. to the northern side of Duyfken Point' as one language.

sources.citation: Hale, Kenneth L. 1964. Classification of Northern Paman languages, Cape York Peninsula, Australia: a research report. Oceanic Linguistics 3(2): 248-265.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: For Northern Paman as a group (p. 256): 'Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it, is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems.' Same group-level statement as Hale 1966 (already in our bibliography, judged not to cover Yangathimri because it is not among the samples); not attributable to Yangathimri under the identity rule, the more so because Crowley 1981: 155-156 describes initial (alternating) stress for the closest sister Mpakwithi/Anguthimri.

sources.citation: McConnel, Ursula H. 1936. Totemic hero-cults in Cape York Peninsula, North Queensland [Part I]. Oceania 6(4): 452-477.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone. p. 455: children of the northern tribes 'tend to say pf and bv for f and v, because the former sounds exist in their language; and have no difficulty in pronouncing s' unlike the Wik tribes; 'Groups of such initial consonants as ndr and mb, which are common in the northern languages do not occur in the Wik languages'; all tribes north and south of the Archer 'use exclusive and inclusive dual and plural pronominal forms.. (which was noted by Dr. Thomson in the Tyoyandyi tribe on the Batavia River)'; 'I have not analysed the languages of the northern tribes'.

sources.citation: Mathew, John. 1899. Eaglehawk and Crow: a study of the Australian Aborigines, including an inquiry into their origin and a survey of Australian languages. London: David Nutt; Melbourne: Melville, Mullen & Slade. Comparative table pp. 208-272, row 'Mapoon R., Q.' (contributed by Revs J. Ward and N. Hey, foreword p. 206).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing for the Mapoon list: the table forms carry no accent marks (checked on the p. 262 page image: njee 'no', iange 'I', tamre 'mine'). The book's only accent sentence, 'The accent usually falls upon the first syllable, which is also the main radical' (general chapter 'Australian Languages', c. pp. 153-154, in a paragraph about Victorian/West Australian and Australian languages at large), is a continent-wide generalisation, not an observation about Mapoon speech, and is not attributable to Yangathimri.
